And it happened at the end of two full years.
Two years.
After the cup-bearer forgot him.
Two years in the pit.
The Cup of waiting held, and held, and held.
Not for a week.
Not for a month.
Two full years.
The man who interpreted dreams sat in a prison while the dream of his own life,
the sheaves, the stars, waited unfulfilled.
The Cup that was poured out in service was left in the dark.
The vessel that held the interpretation held nothing anyone wanted.
For two years.
Then Pharaoh dreamed.
Seven fat cows came up from the Nile.
Beautiful.
Healthy.
Grazing in the marsh grass.
Then seven thin cows, ugly, gaunt, standing beside the fat ones.
The thin ate the fat.
And they looked the same afterward, still thin.
Pharaoh woke.
He slept again.
Seven good ears of grain on one stalk.
Then seven thin, scorched, east-wind ears.
The thin ate the good.
Pharaoh woke.
It was a dream.
Morning came.
Pharaoh's spirit was troubled.
He called all the magicians and wise men of Egypt.
He told them the dreams.
No one could interpret.
No one.
The same word as chapter forty, there is no interpreter.
In all of Egypt, the land of magicians and wise men,
the land of dream interpretation as a science,
no one could read what God had written in Pharaoh's sleep.
The Cup of interpretation was still in the prison.
Still held by a man no one remembered.
Then the cup-bearer spoke.
I remember my sins today.
The cup-bearer.
The man who forgot.
The man whose dream was about a cup, the cup he served,
the cup he lost,
the cup that was restored to him by a prisoner's interpretation.
He remembers.
Two years late.
But he remembers.
Pharaoh was angry with his servants and put me in custody in the house of the captain of the guard,
with the chief baker.
We dreamed a dream in one night, he and I.
There was with us there a young man, a Hebrew,
servant to the captain of the guard.
We told him, and he interpreted to us our dreams.
As he interpreted to us, so it was.
He restored me to my office, and he hanged him.
The forgetting of chapter forty breaks, not by Joseph's action,
not by God's dramatic intervention,
but by a dream Pharaoh has and a servant who finally opens his mouth.
The Cup of waiting is ended by a cup-bearer who remembers his sins.
The man whose job is the cup remembers the man who filled it with meaning.
Then Pharaoh sent and called Joseph.
They brought him hastily out of the dungeon.
He shaved himself.
He changed his clothing.
And he came in to Pharaoh.
The fourth garment.
The coat of many colors, stripped by brothers.
The garment, grabbed by the wife.
The prison clothes, now removed.
Each garment change marks a transition in the Cup's journey.
This time Joseph puts on new clothes himself.
He is not stripped.
He is not seized.
He is being prepared to stand before a king.
The vessel that was undressed by violence is now dressed for elevation.
Pharaoh said: I have dreamed a dream,
and there is no one who can interpret it.
I have heard it said of you that when you hear a dream you can interpret it.
Joseph answered Pharaoh: Not in me.
God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace.
Not in me.
The same posture.
Chapter forty: Do not interpretations belong to God?
Chapter forty one: Not in me.
God will answer.
Joseph never claims the gift.
Not in the pit, not in the prison, not before a king.
The vessel points to the source.
The Cup that holds the interpretation is transparent, the content is God's,
not Joseph's.
Joseph interpreted.
Both dreams are one.
What God is about to do, He has shown to Pharaoh.
Seven years of abundance.
Seven years of famine.
The dream was doubled because the thing is fixed by God,
and God is hastening to do it.
The doubling.
The same pattern as Joseph's own dreams in chapter thirty-seven, two dreams,
one meaning.
The sheaves and the stars.
Now Pharaoh's two dreams, cows and grain.
The doubling means certainty.
God speaks twice when the thing is established.
Then Joseph did something unexpected.
He offered a plan.
Let Pharaoh find a discerning and wise man and set him over Egypt.
Collect one-fifth during the good years.
Store it.
It will be a reserve for the famine years,
so that the land may not be cut off by the famine.
Joseph does not just interpret.
He governs.
The Cup does not just receive, it pours.
The vessel that received dreams now pours out administration.
The man who was bought as a slave now proposes economic policy for an empire.
The man who served in a prison now designs a plan for a nation.
The Cup that was held in confinement now overflows with strategy.
The thing was good in the eyes of Pharaoh and in the eyes of all his servants.
Pharaoh said to his servants: Can we find a man like this,
in whom is the Spirit of God?
The Spirit of God..
The same phrase used in Genesis one,
the Spirit of God hovering over the waters.
The same phrase that will rest on Bezalel when he builds the tabernacle.
Now recognized by a pagan king in a Hebrew prisoner.
The recognition crosses every boundary, covenant and pagan, Hebrew and Egyptian,
slave and king.
Pharaoh sees what Potiphar saw, what the prison keeper saw,
what the cup-bearer saw: the Lord is with this man.
But Pharaoh names it more precisely.
Not just blessing.
Not just prosperity.
The Spirit of God.
Pharaoh said to Joseph: Since God has shown you all this,
there is no one as discerning and wise as you.
You shall be over my house.
All my people shall order themselves by your word.
Only the throne, I am greater than you.
Pharaoh took his ring from his hand and put it on Joseph's hand.
He clothed him in garments of fine linen.
He put a gold chain around his neck.
He had him ride in the second chariot.
Men cried out before him: Bow the knee.
The ring.
Judah gave his seal away in sin,
to a woman he thought was a prostitute.
Now Pharaoh gives his ring to Joseph in elevation.
The seal that was lost in the scandal returns in the elevation.
Identity, taken, given, stolen across three generations,
is now restored by a pagan king who recognizes the Spirit of God.
The ring that Judah surrendered to Tamar is replaced by the ring Pharaoh places on Joseph.
The seal that was lost in disgrace is found in glory.
Fine linen.
The prison clothes are gone.
The coat that was stripped by brothers is replaced by robes given by a king.
The garment that was grabbed by a wife is replaced by a garment that cannot be taken.
Gold chain.
The neck that Rebekah's nurse was buried under, Allon Bacuth,
Oak of Weeping, now wears gold.
The second chariot.
The man who walked to Dothan on foot looking for his brothers now rides behind a king.
Bow the knee.
The man whose brothers refused to speak peaceably to him now hears a nation bow.
Joseph was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh,
king of Egypt.
Thirty.
The same age David will be when he begins to reign.
The same age a priest begins his service.
Seventeen when he was sold.
Thirty when he is elevated.
Thirteen years between the pit and the palace.
Thirteen years of serving, being stripped, being falsely accused, being imprisoned,
interpreting dreams, being forgotten.
Thirteen years of the Lord being with him in the dark.
Joseph went out over all Egypt.
The seven good years came.
The earth produced by handfuls.
He collected all the food of the seven years and stored it,
in the cities,
the food of the field that was around each city,
he stored in it.
Joseph gathered grain like the sand of the sea, very much,
until he stopped counting, for it was beyond number.
Like the sand of the sea.
The echo of God's promise to Abraham:
I will make your offspring as the sand of the sea.
The grain Joseph stores is as uncountable as the descendants God promised.
The Cup that was sold for twenty pieces of silver now holds grain beyond counting.
The promise that was spoken as dust and stars is now stored as wheat and barley.
The covenant that was carried by a family of twelve now feeds an empire.
Two sons were born to Joseph before the famine came.
Asenath, daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, bore them to him.
Joseph called the name of the firstborn Manasseh,
all my hardship and all my father's house.
For God has made me forget Forget.
The cup of waiting produced forgetting, not of the covenant,
but of the pain.
God made me forget.
Not by erasing the memory but by filling the vessel with so much new that the old wounds are carried differently.
The name Manasseh means forget,
but the name itself remembers what was forgotten.
The cup of elevation carries the scars of every descent.
You cannot name a son forget without remembering what you are forgetting.
He called the name of the second Ephraim,
the land of my affliction.
For God has made me fruitful in Fruitful.
Not in the promised land.
Not in the father's house.
Not in Canaan, where the covenant was spoken.
In the land of affliction.
In Egypt.
In the place where he was sold, imprisoned, and forgotten.
God made him fruitful there.
The Cup that was carried out of Canaan into Egypt by force is now full,
not in spite of Egypt, but through Egypt.
The vessel that was stripped and sold and imprisoned is now the vessel through which all the earth is fed.
Then the seven years of plenty ended.
And the seven years of famine began, as Joseph had said.
There was famine in all the lands.
But in all the land of Egypt there was bread.
When all the land of Egypt was famished,
the people cried to Pharaoh for bread.
Pharaoh said to all Egypt: Go to Joseph.
What he says to you, do.
Go to Joseph.
The man who was sold by his brothers is now the only man who has bread.
The man who was stripped is now the man who feeds.
The man who was forgotten is now the man everyone remembers.
The Cup that was thrown into a pit is now the only Cup in the world that holds grain.
The famine was over all the face of the earth.
Joseph opened all the storehouses and sold grain to Egypt.
And the famine was severe in the land of Egypt.
And all the earth came to Egypt to buy grain from Joseph,
because the famine was severe in all the earth.
All the earth.
The dream of chapter thirty-seven, the sheaves bowing, begins its fulfillment.
The brothers who said:
We will see what will become of his dreams,
are about to see.
The stars that bowed in a seventeen-year-old's dream are now walking toward Egypt on foot,
hungry, looking for grain.
The Cup that went down is now over all.
The Cup that was stripped is now robed.
The Cup that was forgotten is now the only Cup anyone comes to.
The man who said here I am to his father and walked toward his brothers is now the man all the earth comes to.
The vessel that was emptied is now full.
The vessel that was thrown away is now the only one that holds.
The Cup of elevation carries the scars of every descent.
The pit.
The prison.
The forgetting.
The two years of silence after the cup-bearer's promise.
None of it is erased.
None of it is cleaned up.
Manasseh means forget, but the name remembers.
Ephraim means fruitful, but the fruitfulness grew in affliction.
The Cup that rises is the same Cup that went down.
It is just fuller.
The vessel that was cracked at every level, stripped, grabbed, imprisoned, forgotten,
is now the vessel that holds grain for the world.
The dream was real.
The waiting was real.
The forgetting was real.
The elevation is real.
And the brothers, the ten who could not speak peaceably to him,
who stripped his coat, who sold him for silver,
who dipped the coat in goat's blood and lied to their father,
are coming.
Hungry.
To the brother they threw away.
The Cup holds.
And it is about to be poured into the vessels that cracked it.
